# Cross-Entropy as a Loss Function and Its Connection to MLE

Cross-entropy bridges information theory and maximum likelihood estimation, providing both the loss function used to train virtually every modern classifier and a rigorous probabilistic justification for why that loss is the right one.

## Definition of Cross-Entropy

$$H(p,q) = -\sum_x p(x)\log q(x) = \mathbb{E}_p[-\log q(X)]$$

Measures average bits needed to encode samples from $p$ using a code optimised for $q$. Since we are using the wrong distribution, $H(p,q) \geq H(p)$ always.

## Decomposition: Cross-Entropy = Entropy + KL

$$H(p,q) = H(p) + \text{KL}(p\|q)$$

- $H(p)$: irreducible entropy of the true labels — fixed by data
- $\text{KL}(p\|q)$: what training can minimise
- Minimising cross-entropy over $q$ is identical to minimising $\text{KL}(p\|q)$

## Connection to Maximum Likelihood Estimation

$$\mathcal{L} = -\frac{1}{N}\sum_i \log q(x_i)$$

This is the empirical cross-entropy and the negative log-likelihood simultaneously. **Maximising log-likelihood = minimising cross-entropy** against the empirical distribution $\hat{p}$.

## Binary Cross-Entropy Loss

$$\text{BCE}(y, q) = -y\log q - (1-y)\log(1-q)$$

## Categorical Cross-Entropy Loss

$$\text{CE}(y, q) = -\sum_k y_k \log q_k = -\log q_c \quad \text{(one-hot labels)}$$

```python
import torch
import torch.nn.functional as F

# Binary cross-entropy
y = torch.tensor([1.0, 0.0, 1.0, 0.0])
q = torch.tensor([0.9, 0.2, 0.7, 0.1])
q_clamped = q.clamp(1e-7, 1 - 1e-7)
bce_manual = -(y * q_clamped.log() + (1-y) * (1-q_clamped).log()).mean()
print(bce_manual)            # matches F.binary_cross_entropy
print(F.binary_cross_entropy(q, y))

# Categorical cross-entropy — stable via log-softmax
logits  = torch.tensor([[2.0, 1.0, 0.5],[0.5, 2.5, 0.0]])
targets = torch.tensor([0, 1])
loss = F.cross_entropy(logits, targets)   # uses subtract-max trick internally
print(loss)
```

## Why Cross-Entropy Over MSE for Classification

- **Gradient saturation:** MSE gradient $\propto (\sigma(f)-y)\sigma'(f)$ saturates near 0/1 predictions. CE gradient $= \sigma(f)-y$ never saturates.
- **Probabilistic calibration:** CE directly optimises the probability of the correct class.
- **Convexity:** CE + softmax is convex in logits per example. MSE + sigmoid is not.
- **MLE optimality:** CE training has asymptotic efficiency, consistency, and Fisher-bound properties from MLE theory.

## Label Smoothing as Changing the Target Distribution

$$p_{\text{smooth}}(k) = (1-\varepsilon)\cdot\mathbf{1}[k=c] + \frac{\varepsilon}{K}$$

Replaces one-hot targets with a softer distribution ($\varepsilon \approx 0.1$). Increases $H(p)$ from 0 to $\approx \varepsilon\log K$, discouraging the model from being overconfident and improving calibration.

## Perplexity as Exponentiated Cross-Entropy

$$\text{PPL} = \exp\!\left(-\frac{1}{N}\sum_i \log q(x_i)\right)$$

Interpretable as the average branching factor. Typical high-quality LLMs: PPL ≈ 5–20.

| Loss Variant | Formula | When to Use |
|---|---|---|
| Binary CE | −(y log q + (1−y) log(1−q)) | Binary / multi-label |
| Categorical CE | −log q_c | Single-label K-class |
| Label-Smoothed CE | −(1−ε) log q_c − (ε/K) Σlog q_k | Prevent overconfidence |
| Weighted CE | −w_c log q_c | Class imbalance |
| Focal Loss | −(1−q_c)^γ log q_c | Hard example mining |

> **TIP: MLE Equivalence — The Core Insight**
> Minimising $H(p_{\text{data}}, q_{\text{model}})$ is exactly MLE. Every result from MLE theory (consistency, efficiency, Fisher information bounds) applies directly to cross-entropy training.

> **WARNING: Cross-Entropy Is Not Symmetric**
> $H(p,q) \neq H(q,p)$. Standard training uses $H(p_{\text{data}}, q_{\text{model}})$ — mode-covering, penalising missed modes. This is the forward KL direction.
